title: The Drug That Met Two Enzymes — 1952 Sea View Isoniazid Breakthrough, Mycobacterial KatG Radical Activation & InhA–INH-NAD Adduct (PDB 1ZID), Xpert MTB/RIF vs. Host NAT2 Acetylator Pharmacogenomics & Azuma Trial Dosing

teenKit.tldr: In 15 seconds: Tuberculosis drug isoniazid meets two enzymes: a bacterial enzyme (KatG) that activates it into a deadly NADH-like warhead inside PDB 1ZID, and a human liver enzyme (NAT2) whose speed determines whether the patient gets cured safely or suffers nerve and liver toxicity.
teenKit.whyItMatters: Half the world carries 'slow acetylator' NAT2 genetics while others are 'rapid acetylators,' meaning a single one-size-fits-all TB dose overexposes some patients and underdoses others.
keyTakeaways: Isoniazid is a prodrug: Mycobacterium tuberculosis catalase-peroxidase KatG oxidizes it into an acyl radical that couples with NAD+ to form INH-NAD, locking mycolic-acid synthase InhA (PDB 1ZID).
Rapid molecular diagnostics (Xpert MTB/RIF and katG/inhA line probes) detect resistance weeks before slow mycobacterial cultures grow.

Human hepatic NAT2 acetylates isoniazid; NAT2 slow acetylators accumulate high parent drug levels (raising hepatotoxicity and B6-depletion neuropathy risk), whereas rapid acetylators risk subtherapeutic exposure—validated in the PGx-guided Azuma trial.

vocab.meaning: An inactive medication that must be chemically transformed by an enzyme before locking onto its target.
Enoyl-acyl carrier protein reductase in M. tuberculosis, essential for building cell-wall mycolic acids.
Human N-acetyltransferase 2, the polymorphic liver enzyme that clears isoniazid.

quiz.question: How does isoniazid block cell-wall synthesis inside Mycobacterium tuberculosis (PDB 1ZID)?
options: It binds intact directly to bacterial ribosomes
Bacterial KatG activates it to form a covalent INH-NAD adduct that tightly inhibits InhA
Human NAT2 converts it into rifampin
It dissolves cholesterol in human macrophages
quiz.explanation: KatG generates an isonicotinoyl radical that reacts with NAD+ to form the picomolar InhA inhibitor INH-NAD.
